The signals of the three models are averages over posterior draws of the participant (Nexus 50, alternative models 200). Within participants, Nexus surprise correlates .67 with the surprise of the change-point observer and .43 with that of the n-state model; the model-free error correlates .38 to .49 with the three surprise signals.

Mixed models of the feedback and the attack pupil: pupil ~ signal (within-participant z) + participant mean of the signal + blocked + trial + condition, random intercept and random slope of the signal per participant, maximum likelihood. All models are fitted on the same trials (feedback pupil 10,160 trials, attack pupil 11,412).
n-state model: switch or new state

Every model signal relates to the feedback pupil (all p < .001), and the surprise of the change-point observer describes it somewhat better than the surprise of Nexus (ΔAIC −69). The model-free error relative to the participant’s own nets describes it far better than any model signal (ΔAIC −755). With the three surprise signals and the model-free error entered together, only the model-free error keeps a contribution (β = 0.188, p < .001; Nexus 0.009, p = .28; change-point observer 0.012, p = .23; n-state model 0.004, p = .60). The attack pupil is smaller after larger errors, most clearly for the model-free error.

The participant’s own placement is the most direct trace of what they expected, so the feedback pupil follows how far the outcome lay from the participant’s own expectation. None of the three models describes the trial-by-trial pupil better than that, and the models do not differ in a way that singles out one of them.

Per participant, the slope of the feedback pupil on each signal (OLS with blocked as covariate, at least 20 trials, per SD of the signal), related to the general factor and STICSA trait (OLS with condition, HC3; 84 participants with scores). A second slope per model signal controls the model-free error.

Slopes are SD of the participant’s pupil coupling per SD of the score. Higher scorers have a stronger feedback-pupil response to surprising outcomes under every model. The association is about as strong for the surprise of the change-point observer and for the state changes of the n-state model as for the surprise of Nexus, and it is weaker for the model-free error. With the model-free error controlled, the association passes the correction for the n-state switches (general factor 0.31, q = .007; STICSA trait 0.34, q = .001) and for the change-point observer’s surprise with STICSA trait (0.35, q = .013); for the general factor it is 0.31 (q = .051) for the change-point observer and 0.36 (q = .073) for Nexus.

The link between the scores and the pupil is carried by surprise as defined by a model of the task’s statistics, and three different models give nearly the same result. The data do not single out the latent-state mechanism of Nexus.
Model-based beyond the participant’s own error.

The pupil itself follows the participant’s own prediction error most closely, but the part of the pupil response that relates to the scores is the part that follows how unexpected an outcome is under the task’s statistics, beyond the distance to the participant’s own nets. Higher scorers’ pupils respond more to outcomes that are statistically surprising, with the participant’s own expectation held constant.

The model-based pupil couplings predict the scores better than the model-free pupil summaries because they index this sensitivity to statistically surprising outcomes. Any of the three models provides such an index; the choice among them does not change the association.

children.value: averaged over posterior draws. Within participants, Nexus state uncertainty and predictive entropy correlate .78; the uncertainty signals of different models correlate .28 to .42, and the entropy of the participant’s own allocation correlates at most .11 with any model signal.

The model uncertainties change slowly over the session (the number of states of the n-state model mostly grows), so the models use 20-trial bins instead of a linear trial term. With a linear trial term, the number of states takes over the slow decline of the baseline pupil (β = −0.11, z = −6.3); with the bins it does not (β = −0.03, p = .095).
(mixed models as above; β per SD of the signal within participants; ISI 10,630 trials, baseline 12,746, anticipation 11,817, placement 13,515; 85 participants):

children.value: q = .007, entropy q = .013); the n-state model (q = .094) and Nexus (q ≥ .21) point the same way without passing the correction. During the placement of the nets, the pupil is smaller when Nexus and the change-point observer are more uncertain (all four q ≤ .011). No signal relates to the baseline after correction (all q ≥ .31). With the Nexus signals, the change-point observer’s entropy, the n-state model’s entropy and the own allocation entropy entered together, the ISI pupil keeps a positive contribution of the change-point observer’s entropy (0.013, p = .012) and a negative one of the own allocation entropy (−0.020, p < .001).

Within the conditions (family: one signal in the three conditions), the ISI slope is positive for the n-state model’s uncertainty with partial instructions (0.025, q = .019; entropy 0.028, q = .012); for Nexus state uncertainty without instructions (0.018, p = .036, q = .11) and the change-point observer’s entropy with full instructions (0.021, p = .023, q = .070) it does not pass the correction. With full instructions the ISI pupil is smaller when the participant’s own allocation is more spread (−0.035, q = .013). The baseline pupil is lower with more states of the n-state model with partial instructions (−0.15, q = .001) and not in the other conditions.

Per participant, the slope of the ISI pupil on each signal (also controlling the entropy of the own allocation) was related to the general factor and STICSA trait as above (83 participants). children.value: The anticipatory pupil follows model uncertainty only weakly (β ≤ 0.016 per SD in the ISI, against 0.06 to 0.11 for the surprise signals of the three models in the feedback window), and the uncertainty of the change-point observer describes it at least as well as that of Nexus.
The entropy of the participant’s own allocation, the model-free counterpart, does not increase the ISI pupil; with full instructions a wider spread of the own nets goes with a smaller ISI pupil.

Unlike the response to surprising outcomes, the coupling of the pupil with uncertainty before the outcome carries no individual differences related to the scores. The score-related pupil signal is the response to the outcome, not the state of uncertainty while waiting for it.

The feedback screen (2.0 s) shows outcome-specific animations: after a bite a full-screen red flash fading over 0.8 s, a screen shake for 0.5 s and a pulsing “BITE!”; after a block a green glow until 2.0 s, sparkles until 1.2 s and “BLOCKED!”. The standard feedback window (500 to 2500 ms) overlaps all of them, and larger errors go with bites. The surprise comparison was therefore repeated (
in sub-windows of the feedback epoch with the same pre-feedback baseline: early 500 to 1500 ms, late 1500 to 2500 ms, and after the feedback screen 2000 to 3000 ms (the epochs end at 3000 ms);
on the next trial: anticipation pupil (cue + 1500 to 4000 ms, own pre-cue baseline) and pre-cue baseline pupil of trial t + 1, when it directly follows t;
within bite trials only and within blocked trials only, so that the animation is identical on every trial of an analysis.
The models use 20-trial bins and the condition as covariates (and blocked in the analyses of all trials).
(β per SD of the signal within participants, p):
Trials: about 10,200 to 11,000 in all, 7,000 to 7,800 bites and 2,900 to 3,250 blocks per window.

The surprise response is a response to bites. Within bites, where the flash, the shake and the text are the same on every trial, the pupil is larger the more surprising the bite, under every model and for the model-free error. Within blocks the relation is weakly negative.

The surprise response grows from the early to the late part of the feedback and is as large after the feedback screen has ended (2000 to 3000 ms). It is therefore not the light response to the early flash.
The surprise of trial t does not carry over into the anticipation or the baseline pupil of the next trial (model signals all p ≥ .24).

Correction (Benjamini-Hochberg; family: the four signals of one window in one trial subset): all model signals in the feedback windows within bites have q < .001; within blocks only the model-free error passes (feedback window q = .002) and the change-point observer’s surprise after the screen (q = .044); the next-trial windows have no term with q < .05.

(slope of the participant’s pupil on the signal, per SD of the general factor; HC3, 83 to 84 participants; p in the table). Correction (Benjamini-Hochberg; per trial subset, window and score, the four slopes are one family, the three slopes controlling the model-free error another): in all trials and in all bites, every model signal in the three feedback windows has q ≤ .044; in blocks none has q < .19.

Within bites, with the model-free error controlled, the slopes are 0.31 (Nexus, p = .054, q = .082), 0.20 (change-point observer, p = .12, q = .12) and 0.26 (n-state switches, p = .010, q = .031) in the full window, and 0.28 (q = .086), 0.19 (q = .086) and 0.32 (q = .009) after the feedback screen. A bite happens either because no net was in the attack slot (the allocation missed the attack direction; 6,848 trials, median 77 per participant) or although at least one net was in the attack slot (the attack got through a correct allocation; 2,217 trials, median 25 per participant, range 5 to 62). The two kinds have the same animation.
(β per SD of the signal within participants, p):

At the same surprise, the pupil after a bite despite a net is smaller than after a bite without a net (Nexus surprise controlled: −0.48 in the feedback window, −0.57 late, −0.56 after the screen, all p < .001; the same with the other signals and with the model-free error controlled, −0.31 to −0.38). The next trial’s baseline pupil is also smaller after a bite despite a net (−0.17, p < .001), and its anticipation pupil slightly larger (0.05, p = .013).

The pupil response is therefore not a response to being bitten as such: it is large when the bite shows that the allocation missed the attack, and it scales with how surprising the attack was only then. When the attack came where the nets were and got through anyway, the pupil is smaller and does not follow surprise.

Participants with at least 12 bites of the kind (despite a net: 65 to 74 participants; without a net: 83 to 84). Correction as above: within bites without a net, the three model signals have q ≤ .048 in the feedback and late windows (after the screen only the n-state switches, q = .026); within bites despite a net all q ≥ .42. Within bites without a net and with the model-free error controlled, the slopes are 0.28 (Nexus, p = .027), 0.16 (change-point observer, p = .12) and 0.19 (n-state switches, p = .070) in the feedback window and 0.28, 0.19 and 0.24 (p = .024, .046, .033) in the late window. STICSA trait gives the same pattern (Nexus 0.27, p = .012; change-point observer 0.26, p = .010; n-state switches 0.28, p = .003 in the feedback window).

Per participant, the mean pupil after bites despite a net minus that after bites without a net (at least 12 of each) is −0.49 in the feedback window; it is smaller with higher scores without p < .05 (general factor −0.20, p = .11; early window −0.21, p = .073; family per score: the four feedback windows, all q ≥ .18). The corresponding difference in the next trial’s baseline is smaller with higher STICSA trait scores (−0.24, p = .044, q = .089; family: the two next-trial windows; general factor −0.17, p = .085).

The association of the scores with the pupil response to surprising outcomes holds within bite trials, where the animation is constant, and after the feedback screen has ended. It is therefore not produced by the animations. It is a response to surprising bites that show a missed prediction: bites that got through a correct allocation and blocked outcomes carry it only weakly (about 25 and 38 such trials per participant). A remaining difference between trials that this control does not address is the gaze position at the outcome: after a surprising attack the participant may look further from the screen centre, which changes the measured pupil size; a check needs the gaze samples of the feedback epoch.
